story.headline: Iran threatens neighbours over US economic war
story.summary: Iran warned neighbouring states they will be treated as enemies if they join a US-led economic campaign, threatening Gulf oil routes, as Washington readied fresh sanctions.
story.display_body: Iran warned neighbouring states on Saturday 22 August that they would be treated as "enemies" if they join a US-led economic campaign, and threatened the region's oil-shipping routes, as Washington prepared fresh sanctions. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said any country taking part in imposing economic restrictions "will be regarded as an enemy," describing a staged response ending in what he called a "seismic" retaliation and raising the prospect of Iran targeting Gulf oil corridors that serve as alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz (the narrow chokepoint carrying roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil), which Tehran closed after the joint US–Israeli strikes of 28 February 2026. The threats followed US President Donald Trump's vow of what he termed the "most crushing economic operation" against Iran and "tremendous economic consequences" for nations offering Tehran "any type of lifeline"; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent framed it as "you're either with us or against us" — a line aimed largely at China, which buys the bulk of Iran's exported oil — and is due to detail specific measures on Monday 24 August. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, dismissed the pressure as a "diversion" from America's own fiscal strains and said it "will only bring further defeat." Nearly six months into the war and a naval blockade, Iran's economy is under severe strain, and independent confirmation of the rival claims is limited.
story.why: an explicit US "with-us-or-against-us" sanctions doctrine puts trade-dependent, neutrality-minded states — Switzerland among them — under pressure to pick sides, and any Iranian move against Gulf shipping would ripple straight into global energy prices.

story.headline: Kazakhstan votes in tightly controlled election
story.summary: Kazakhstan held a parliamentary election on 23 August expected to cement President Tokayev's grip, with only state-approved parties allowed to run.
story.display_body: Kazakhstan voted on Sunday 23 August in a parliamentary election widely expected to entrench President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's control of Central Asia's largest state. Polls opened at 7am local time and were due to close at 8pm (15:00 GMT), choosing a new 145-seat single-chamber legislature under a constitutional overhaul that bars parties not approved by the authorities. The pro-presidential Adilet party is forecast to win a commanding majority, with several smaller loyalist parties also expected to enter parliament; no genuine opposition is standing. Tokayev has led the oil-rich country since 2019.
story.why: the vote formalises a managed political system in a state that Russia, China and the EU all court for energy and transit, so who sits in parliament shapes little but the balance Astana strikes between those powers matters a great deal.

story.headline: Myanmar airstrike kills 14 at monastery
story.summary: A Myanmar military airstrike killed at least 14 mostly elderly civilians at a Buddhist monastery in Sagaing during a meditation retreat, opposition and witnesses say.
story.display_body: A Myanmar military airstrike killed at least 14 people at a Buddhist monastery in the central Sagaing region on Friday 21 August, opposition and witness accounts say. The strike hit Swel Le Oh village in Myaung township, about 75 km west of Mandalay, at around 9am local time while more than 100 mostly elderly people were gathered for a week-long meditation retreat marking Buddhist Lent (Vassa, the monastic rains retreat); the site was reportedly struck twice. Those killed — 11 men and three women, aged roughly 50 to 70 — were civilians, and about 20 were wounded, according to the opposition National Unity Government and local witnesses. Sagaing is a stronghold of armed resistance to the military junta that seized power in 2021, and the army, which has not commented, has repeatedly used air power against populated areas there. This account rests on opposition and witness sources; the military has issued no statement.

story.headline: DR Congo and M23 agree talks roadmap
story.summary: DRC and AFC/M23 negotiators, meeting in Switzerland 17-21 August under the Doha framework, agreed a roadmap for talks; the first EJVM+ ceasefire verification mission is set for 24 August in Minembwe.
story.display_body: The DR Congo government and the AFC/M23 rebel alliance agreed a negotiating roadmap after talks held in Switzerland from 17 to 21 August, mediators announced on Saturday 22 August. In a joint statement, the parties — alongside Qatar, the United States, Togo (the African Union mediator), the AU Commission and Switzerland — said they had "developed a roadmap setting out sequenced steps and timelines" for negotiating the outstanding protocols of the Doha Framework. They welcomed progress on the EJVM+ — the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus, the joint body tasked with monitoring the ceasefire — whose first ceasefire-verification mission is scheduled for Monday 24 August in Minembwe, and agreed to set up a mechanism to track implementation.
story.why: eastern Congo's war has displaced millions, and a working monitoring-and-negotiation track — brokered partly on Swiss soil, underscoring Bern's role in the process — is the first concrete sign of forward motion since the November framework.

story.headline: Two dead in Thusis house fire
story.summary: Rescuers recovered at least two bodies from a house fire in Thusis, Graubunden, with three people still missing; the collapse-prone building is hampering the search.
story.display_body: Rescuers recovered at least two bodies from a house fire in Thusis, in the canton of Graubünden, cantonal police confirmed on Saturday 22 August, with three people still missing. The blaze broke out overnight into Friday 21 August in a building that housed apartments; the structure remains at risk of collapse, which the Graubünden cantonal police said is hampering the search and the investigation, so crews have so far reached only part of the site. Earlier reports had listed five people missing and several injured. The cause is not yet established.

story.headline: Heat brings Switzerland's earliest grape harvest
story.summary: A hot, dry summer has pushed the Swiss grape harvest about three weeks earlier than usual, with picking already under way in August; lower volume but promising quality.
story.display_body: Switzerland's grape harvest is running about three weeks ahead of a normal year, with picking already under way in August after a hot, dry summer. Growers in the Bündner Herrschaft region of Graubünden have begun bringing in grapes, and harvest is expected to start from late August in Schaffhausen and Thurgau and in early September in Vaud — a pace matched only by exceptional years such as 2003 and 2018. Volumes look set to come in below average because of the drought, but vintners describe the quality outlook for 2026 as promising.
story.why: the calendar shift is a concrete, local marker of how repeated heatwaves are reshaping Swiss agriculture, compressing the working year for one of the country's signature crops.
